raw: 7.1 COMINT and ELINT: Definitions and Distinctions[^35]
teaching_note: COMINT concerns intelligence from communications, including content and relevant traffic/metadata; ELINT concerns non-communications electromagnetic emissions such as radar signals, not any electronic file or cryptographic digital signature. An emission's characteristics, an assessed emitter, a person, and intent are progressively different claims, not synonymous observations. **Completed offline synthetic classification:** provided card C contains a fictional message and send time (communications content plus metadata), card E describes an invented radar-like emission (ELINT-type subject matter), and card S reports a document-signature check (cryptographic authentication, not ELINT); none involves actual interception. On challenge, C's timestamp is marked unsynchronized, so the analyst keeps the classification but withdraws the exact event-time inference and holds any consequential timing judgment. The NSA overview supports SIGINT orientation; finer operational definitions/remits need the applicable dated doctrine, and classroom classification creates no authority to acquire signals.
title: COMINT and ELINT: Content, Metadata, and Non-Communication Signals

raw: 7.2 Historical Foundations: WWII Axis SIGINT (NSA Declassified 9 Volumes)[^36]
teaching_note: The inherited NSA catalog identifies a nine-volume European Axis SIGINT collection, which concerns wartime organizations and records rather than a modern operating manual. Separate the historical period described, the authoring body's perspective, archival custody, and later public release; a release date is not the date of the event. The source page was unavailable to direct inspection during this revision, so volume-level findings, completeness, and precise release dates remain unverified here. The defensible result is an identified historical collection and a bounded extraction plan, not assertions about unexamined volumes or a reconstruction of collection techniques.
title: European Axis SIGINT Records: Wartime Scope and Archival Limits

raw: 7.3 Spartans in Darkness: SIGINT in the Indochina War, 1945–1975[^37]
teaching_note: The inherited citation is a report about release of Robert J. Hanyok's historical study covering 1945–1975, not itself the complete underlying history or every contemporaneous intercept. A retrospective historian's reconstruction, a wartime report, and a policymaker's later testimony answer different evidentiary questions and must not be merged. In particular, an article summarizing a Tonkin conclusion cannot by itself prove the event claim or certify the full record's completeness; a historical judgment needs its identified passage, source basis, redactions, and alternatives examined. The supported classroom disposition is attributed secondary reporting with the underlying-event conclusion held pending the original record, not an unqualified historical verdict.
title: Spartans in Darkness: Retrospective History versus Contemporaneous Reporting

teaching_note: The inspected 20 March 2015 National Security Archive briefing distinguishes its editorial account from the declassified documents and identifies a CIA SIGINT history covering 1947–1970 [@ageint039]. Its Document 2 is an Inspector General memorandum dated 22 August 1958, identified with CREST/NARA provenance; the archive describes Division D as a conduit for communications intelligence from NSA to CIA, illustrating that production, receipt, and institutional custody are distinct roles. This is an attributed archival description, not a fresh examination of the full memorandum or a present-day authority chart; author identity and missing/redacted content must remain unknown where withheld. The inherited 2018 blog is secondary context, not independent corroboration of the same underlying documents, and no collection technique is reconstructed.
title: CIA–NSA Historical Roles: Document Dates, Coordination, and Redactions

teaching_note: In introductory historical vocabulary, a code substitutes representations for units of meaning using an agreed vocabulary, while a cipher transforms message symbols according to a rule, often controlled by a key; ordinary language can blur the distinction. Neither the label nor archival hosting establishes modern security, authenticity, or factual truth. Record the original title/author/date where available and distinguish them from release metadata; the inherited clipped sentence is not enough to establish the text's complete technical argument or period of applicability. A diagnostic answer rejects 'NSA-hosted therefore currently secure' and separates an archival teaching object from an approved modern algorithm and key-management system. No live decoding, interception, covert communication construction, or operational reuse is part of the lesson.
title: Friedman Cryptography Records: Historical Concepts, Not Modern Security Advice
